# Lecture 2: What the model assumes and how residuals reveal it {#i02} ::: {.outcomes} By the end of Lecture 2, you can - explain what the main assumptions of a regression are needed for - check the main assumptions of a regression with residual plots - say which assumptions need knowledge of the data rather than plots - find influential observations and handle them openly and carefully ::: ::: {.driving-question} Driving question

Linear regression is a model with assumptions. The estimates, standard errors, tests, and intervals of Lectures 1 and 3 are reliable only when these assumptions hold, at least approximately. R fits the line and prints the output in any case. It does not check the assumptions for you automatically. You check them yourself, with plots and with knowledge of how the data were collected.

The fitted line from Lecture 1 looks convincing. Under what conditions should we trust it, and what do its residuals reveal? ::: ::: {.course-phase .phase-before} ## Before class Do all the preparation below before class.
No video this week
The preparation for this lecture is your own residual plot. Do the R warm-up below and bring the plot to class.
**Predict.** Answer this question before you come to class: the agreed valuations are strongly right-skewed (most are small and a few are very large), far from a normal distribution. Does that alone make the Lecture 1 regression of the agreed valuation on the claimed valuation invalid, yes or no? Choose one answer before class and write one sentence explaining why. The lecture material gives the correct answer. [Shark Tank data]{.shark-tag} **R warm-up.** Rebuild the Lecture 1 model, the regression of the agreed valuation on the claimed valuation (both in \$ millions) for the 874 deals for a share of the company. Make its residual-versus-fitted plot: the fitted values on the horizontal axis and the residuals on the vertical axis. Bring the plot to class: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} sharks <- read.csv("data/shark_tank_teaching.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE) vals <- subset(sharks, deal_on_show == 1 & deal_equity_pct > 0) vals$claimed_m <- vals$requested_valuation_usd / 1e6 vals$agreed_m <- vals$deal_valuation_usd / 1e6 val_model <- lm(agreed_m ~ claimed_m, data = vals) plot(fitted(val_model), residuals(val_model)) abline(h = 0, lty = 2) ``` ::: **Code along (bring your laptop).** Bring a charged laptop with RStudio and the course project open, so that you can run the code of this chapter yourself during the lecture and get the same numbers and figures. ::: ::: {.course-phase .phase-in-class} ## Lecture material This section states what the regression model assumes. It then shows how to check these assumptions with the residuals of the Lecture 1 model. It also shows which assumptions no plot can check. ### Start with a founder's question [Shark Tank data]{.shark-tag} Lecture 1 gave you a number: each extra dollar of claimed valuation goes with about 65 cents more agreed valuation, on average. Before you plan a negotiation around this number, ask whether you can trust the line behind it. R draws a line through any data, even through data that do not support a line. R never warns you. ### The residual plot from the warm-up [Shark Tank data]{.shark-tag} The code below is the warm-up code. It rebuilds the data and the model of Lecture 1: the valuation agreed on air (`agreed_m`) regressed on the valuation claimed by the founder (`claimed_m`), both in \$ millions, for the 874 Shark Tank deals for a share of the company. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} sharks <- read.csv("data/shark_tank_teaching.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE) vals <- subset(sharks, deal_on_show == 1 & deal_equity_pct > 0) vals$claimed_m <- vals$requested_valuation_usd / 1e6 vals$agreed_m <- vals$deal_valuation_usd / 1e6 val_model <- lm(agreed_m ~ claimed_m, data = vals) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="See the R code for this figure"} library(ggplot2) sharks <- read.csv("data/shark_tank_teaching.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE) vals <- subset(sharks, deal_on_show == 1 & deal_equity_pct > 0) vals$claimed_m <- vals$requested_valuation_usd / 1e6 vals$agreed_m <- vals$deal_valuation_usd / 1e6 val_model <- lm(agreed_m ~ claimed_m, data = vals) resid_df <- data.frame( fitted = fitted(val_model), residual = residuals(val_model) ) ggplot(resid_df, aes(x = fitted, y = residual)) + geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "#C98B2E", linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.8) + geom_point(alpha = 0.45, size = 1.6, colour = "#009E73") + annotate("text", x = 31.5, y = 0.9, label = "residual = 0", hjust = 1, colour = "#17324D", size = 3.4) + labs(x = "Fitted agreed valuation ($ millions)", y = "Residual ($ millions)") + theme_minimal(base_size = 13) + theme( panel.grid.minor = element_blank(), panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(), plot.caption = element_text(colour = "#5B6976"), axis.title = element_text(colour = "#17324D") ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Residuals against fitted values for the Lecture 1 valuation model, both in $ millions. On the left the residuals lie close to zero. On the right they spread over several million dollars.](i02-assumptions-diagnostics_files/figure-html/fig-i02-warmup-residuals-1.png){#fig-i02-warmup-residuals width=672} ::: ::: ::: {.definition-box} Definition **Residual plot** (residual-versus-fitted plot). A scatterplot with the fitted values $\widehat Y_i$ on the horizontal axis and the residuals $e_i$ on the vertical axis. It shows how the residuals change from the left to the right of the plot. ::: In @fig-i02-warmup-residuals, both axes are in the units of the outcome, \$1 million. A point above zero is a deal that was agreed at a higher valuation than its fitted value. A point below zero is a deal that was agreed at a lower valuation than its fitted value. To read patterns in this plot, you first need to know what the model assumes. ### What each assumption supports The model of Lecture 1 is $$ Y_i=\beta_0+\beta_1X_i+\varepsilon_i. $$ Least squares gives a line for any data. Whether the numbers that come with the line are reliable depends on a few assumptions. ::: {.definition-box} Definition **Model assumptions.** Conditions on the data and on the error terms $\varepsilon_i$ under which the estimates, standard errors, tests, and intervals of least squares are reliable. ::: The assumptions are about the error terms $\varepsilon_i$ of the model. We never observe the error terms. The plots in this lecture therefore use the residuals $e_i$, which are our estimates of the error terms (Lecture 1). The table lists each assumption, says how to check it, and says what goes wrong if it fails. | Assumption | What it says in plain words | How to check it | What goes wrong if it fails | |---|---|---|---| | Variation in $X$ | Not all observations have the same value of $X$ | Look at the values of $X$, for example with `summary()` | R cannot calculate a slope | | Linearity | The average of $Y$ at each value of $X$ lies on a straight line: $E[Y\mid X=x]=\beta_0+\beta_1x$ | Residual plot: look for a curve | One slope misses part of the pattern, and the line is wrong in some parts of the range | | Independence (random sampling) | The observations are drawn independently: the error of one row says nothing about the error of another row | Knowledge of how the data were collected | The usual standard errors are often too small, so intervals are too narrow. A sample that is not random can also bias the line | | Homoskedasticity (constant variance) | The errors have the same variance at every value of $X$: $\operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon_i\mid X_i)=\sigma^2$ | Residual plot: look for a fan shape | The slope stays unbiased, but the usual standard errors, tests, and intervals are wrong | | Normality of the errors | At each value of $X$, the errors follow a normal distribution | A normal Q--Q plot of the residuals (explained later in this lecture) | In small samples the t and F distributions of Lecture 3 are no longer exact. In large samples this matters little | | Zero conditional mean (exogeneity): no omitted confounder | The error averages zero at every value of $X$: $E[\varepsilon_i\mid X_i]=0$. For a causal reading: no other cause of $Y$ that is missing from the model is related to $X$ | Knowledge of how $X$ came about. No plot can show it | The slope is not the effect of changing $X$. It still describes how average outcomes differ across values of $X$ | The rows fall into groups. Variation in $X$ is needed before R can calculate a slope at all. In multiple regression (Lecture 4) this condition becomes no perfect multicollinearity. Variation in $X$, linearity, independent observations, and zero conditional mean together make the estimated slope $\hat\beta_1$ unbiased: across many samples, it is correct on average. Homoskedasticity and independence are needed for the usual standard errors, and so for the t-tests and intervals of Lecture 3. Normality of the errors makes these tests and intervals exact in small samples. In large samples they hold approximately without it, because of the central limit theorem. The last row matters for how you read the slope. A **confounder** is a variable that is not in the model and that affects both $X$ and $Y$. If you read the slope only as a description of how average outcomes differ across values of $X$, the error is just the distance from the line of averages. Linearity then already makes the errors average zero at every value of $X$. If you read the slope as the effect of changing $X$, the error term contains all other causes of $Y$. Zero conditional mean then says that these other causes are unrelated to $X$. An omitted confounder breaks this assumption. This is common with observational data such as the Shark Tank deals, where nobody sets $X$ at random. When a confounder is left out, the slope of $X$ also picks up the relationship between the confounder and $Y$. The slope is then too large or too small as a measure of the effect of $X$. This distortion is called **omitted variable bias**. Lecture 4 shows it in an example, and shows how adding the confounder to the model as a control variable removes it. No row of the table says that the data are normal. This answers the prediction question from before class: the outcome does not need to be normally distributed, and neither does the predictor. The agreed valuations are strongly right-skewed, and this skew alone does not break any assumption. The assumptions are about the average of $Y$ at each $X$, about the errors, and about how the data were produced. They are not about the histogram of $Y$ or the histogram of $X$. ### Linearity is about the average, not every point Individual outcomes do not have to lie on a line. Linearity says that the average outcome at each predictor value follows a line. If the residual plot shows a curve, one constant slope misses part of that average pattern. Homoskedasticity is about the vertical spread. It says that the variance of the errors is the same at each predictor value. It does not say that all residuals have the same size. When the variance changes with the predictor, this is called **heteroskedasticity**. In a residual plot, heteroskedasticity often looks like a fan shape: the vertical band of points widens or narrows from left to right. @fig-i02-assumption-panels shows both problems. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="See the R code for this figure"} library(ggplot2) set.seed(802) n_demo <- 90 x_demo <- runif(n_demo, 0, 10) y_linear <- 2 + 0.65 * x_demo + rnorm(n_demo, 0, 0.8) y_curved <- 2 + 0.10 * x_demo + 0.09 * x_demo^2 + rnorm(n_demo, 0, 0.55) m_curved <- lm(y_curved ~ x_demo) m_linear <- lm(y_linear ~ x_demo) fit_demo <- seq(1, 9, length.out = n_demo) # Residual panels drawn as clear textbook cases: an even band for constant # spread, and a band that widens steadily for changing spread. res_constant <- runif(n_demo, -1, 1) res_fan <- runif(n_demo, -1, 1) * (0.1 + 0.22 * fit_demo) panel_names <- c("Linear mean (outcome)", "Curved mean (residuals)", "Constant spread (residuals)", "Changing spread (residuals)") demo_df <- data.frame( panel = factor(rep(panel_names, each = n_demo), levels = panel_names), x = c(x_demo, fitted(m_curved), fit_demo, fit_demo), y = c(y_linear, residuals(m_curved), res_constant, res_fan) ) line_df <- data.frame( panel = factor(panel_names[1], levels = panel_names), intercept = coef(m_linear)[1], slope = coef(m_linear)[2] ) zero_df <- data.frame( panel = factor(panel_names[-1], levels = panel_names), yintercept = 0 ) zero_lab <- data.frame( panel = factor(panel_names[-1], levels = panel_names), x = c(min(fitted(m_curved)), 1, 1), y = c(max(residuals(m_curved)), max(res_constant), max(res_fan)) ) ggplot(demo_df, aes(x = x, y = y)) + geom_hline(data = zero_df, aes(yintercept = yintercept), colour = "#C98B2E", linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.8) + geom_abline(data = line_df, aes(intercept = intercept, slope = slope), colour = "#D55E00", linewidth = 0.9) + geom_point(alpha = 0.45, size = 1.6, colour = "#009E73") + geom_text(data = zero_lab, aes(x = x, y = y, label = "residual = 0"), hjust = 0, colour = "#17324D", size = 3) + facet_wrap(~ panel, scales = "free") + labs(x = "Predictor (top left) or fitted value", y = "Outcome (top left) or residual") + theme_minimal(base_size = 13) + theme( panel.grid.minor = element_blank(), panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(), plot.caption = element_text(colour = "#5B6976"), axis.title = element_text(colour = "#17324D"), strip.text = element_text(colour = "#17324D", face = "bold") ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Four simulated situations. Top row: a linear mean fits (left, outcome against predictor), a curved mean leaves a U-shaped residual pattern (right). Bottom row: constant vertical spread, homoskedasticity (left), spread growing with the fitted value, heteroskedasticity with a fan shape (right). The three residual panels share the gold dashed line at residual zero.](i02-assumptions-diagnostics_files/figure-html/fig-i02-assumption-panels-1.png){#fig-i02-assumption-panels width=672} ::: ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Check: match each residual pattern to the assumption it challenges A U-shaped (curved) residual pattern challenges linearity: the average residual is not zero everywhere, so a straight line misses part of the mean relationship. A fan shape challenges homoskedasticity: the vertical spread of residuals changes with the fitted value. A real plot can show both problems at once. ::: ### Reading the valuation model's vertical spread [Shark Tank data]{.shark-tag} Now look for heteroskedasticity in @fig-i02-warmup-residuals. At small fitted values the residuals stay close to the zero line. At larger fitted values they spread over several million dollars. A short calculation confirms what the plot shows. The code sorts the deals by the claimed valuation into five groups. Each group has about a fifth of the deals. The code then gives the standard deviation of the residuals in each group: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} fifth <- cut(vals$claimed_m, breaks = quantile(vals$claimed_m, probs = seq(0, 1, 0.2)), include.lowest = TRUE) round(tapply(residuals(val_model), fifth, sd), 2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [0.04,0.625] (0.625,1.33] (1.33,2.5] (2.5,5] (5,50] 0.14 0.36 1.19 1.08 3.61 ``` ::: ::: The standard deviation of the residuals is about \$0.14 million in the fifth of deals with the smallest claimed valuations and about \$3.6 million in the fifth with the largest, about 25 times as much. The spread of agreed valuations broadly grows with the size of the claim. This makes economic sense: founders and sharks can disagree by much more money about a \$20 million company than about a \$200,000 company. This pattern is heteroskedasticity. The usual standard errors assume one common variance $\sigma^2$, so here they depend on an assumption that probably does not hold. The slope itself stays unbiased, because heteroskedasticity is not part of the conditions for an unbiased slope. Lecture 3 returns to this point. ::: {.callout-caution collapse="true"} ## Try it: annotate a residual plot [Shark Tank data]{.shark-tag} Try this with your neighbour first. Use a printed copy or a sketch of @fig-i02-warmup-residuals. *Step 1 (given).* The horizontal dashed line marks residual zero. Points above it are deals with an agreed valuation above the fitted value. Points below it are deals with an agreed valuation below the fitted value. *Step 2 (you).* Draw two rough curves around the residuals, one along the top of the points and one along the bottom, from the left edge to the right edge of the plot. Does the band between the two curves stay equally wide? *Step 3 (you).* Name the assumption that your two curves challenge. Then write one sentence that says whether the average of the residuals also moves away from zero in some part of the plot. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Check your answer The band between the two curves widens strongly from left to right. Deals with small fitted valuations lie within a few hundred thousand dollars of the line. Deals with large fitted valuations lie within several million. This fan shape shows heteroskedasticity, so it challenges homoskedasticity. The average residual stays near zero across the range, so the plot does not show a clear violation of linearity. You read the same plot twice, once for each assumption. ::: ::: ### What plots cannot show Two rows of the assumptions table never appear in any residual plot. **Zero conditional mean (no omitted confounder).** A curve in the residual plot can show that a straight line misses the average pattern. No plot can show whether a confounder exists, that is, whether something that is missing from the data affects both the predictor and the outcome. The reason is the difference between errors and residuals. Least squares always gives residuals with a mean of zero and no straight-line relation to $X$, even when the error terms are related to $X$. So the residual plot looks clean even when a confounder exists. Ask how the observations were produced. Which common causes of $X$ and $Y$ are plausible but missing from the data? **Independence.** Whether the errors of different rows are related is a fact about how the data were collected. The residual plot does not show it. Suppose that rows are related but you treat them as independent. Then the data seem to contain more information than they really do, and the standard errors are too small. Two examples from Shark Tank: - **Shared episodes.** Pitches in the same episode face the same panel of sharks on the same day, and the same few sharks appear in hundreds of deals. Their rows share negotiators, moods, and editing decisions. This is an **independence** problem: the 874 deals contain somewhat less information than 874 unrelated deals would. - **Network ties.** Suppose founders with strong investor networks both claim higher valuations (they know the market) and get better deals (the sharks know them). Network strength is not recorded in the data. It is related to the predictor, and it affects the outcome. This is a **confounding** problem: network strength is an omitted confounder, so zero conditional mean fails for a causal reading. The slope still describes how average agreed valuations differ across claims. But you cannot read the slope as what a higher claim would achieve. Neither problem is visible in @fig-i02-warmup-residuals. You can find both problems only if you know how the show works. ### Influence: when a few rows move the line a lot [Shark Tank data]{.shark-tag} A first check needs no plot. The function `summary()` gives the smallest residual, the largest residual, the mean, the median, and the two quartiles. [Basic Lecture 1](../basic/b01-introduction-data-analysis.qmd#b01-quartiles) defines the median and the quartiles: a quarter of the values lie below the first quartile, half below the median, and three quarters below the third quartile. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} summary(residuals(val_model)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Min. 1st Qu. Median Mean 3rd Qu. Max. -7.817198 -0.396788 -0.006381 0.000000 0.173447 13.446138 ``` ::: ::: ::: {#exm-i02-residual-line} ## Worked example: reading the summary of the residuals [Shark Tank data]{.shark-tag} Read the numbers one by one, all in \$ millions: - The **median** residual is about $-0.01$: the typical deal lies almost exactly on the fitted line. - The middle half of all residuals, from the first to the third quartile, runs from $-0.40$ to $0.17$: a band about \$570,000 wide. - The **minimum** is about $-7.8$ and the **maximum** about $13.4$: one deal was agreed \$7.8 million below its fitted valuation and another \$13.4 million above. The mean is zero, as it always is when the model has an intercept. If no deal were extreme, the largest residuals would be a few times the width of the middle half. Here they are 14 to 24 times as large. A few deals miss the line by far more than the typical deal does, and such deals can strongly change the fitted line. The same numbers, without the mean, appear at the top of `summary(val_model)`. Lecture 3 explains this output. ::: Two standard tools make this check precise. A **standardised residual**, `rstandard()`, is a residual divided by its standard deviation, so it measures the residual in standard deviations. Values beyond about $\pm 3$ are large by any common standard. **Cook's distance**, `cooks.distance()`, measures how much the whole fitted line would move if one observation were removed. A common threshold is $4/n$: you look more closely at observations above it. ::: {.definition-box} Definition **Outlier.** An observation with an unusually large residual: its outcome lies far from the fitted line. A common rule is a standardised residual beyond $\pm 3$. **Influential observation.** An observation that changes the fitted line noticeably when it is removed. A common rule is a Cook's distance above $4/n$. ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} rs <- rstandard(val_model) cd <- cooks.distance(val_model) sum(abs(rs) > 3) # standardised residuals beyond 3 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 25 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} sum(cd > 4 / nobs(val_model)) # Cook's distance above 4/n ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 64 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} vals[order(cd, decreasing = TRUE)[1:3], c("claimed_m", "agreed_m")] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` claimed_m agreed_m 1075 50 25 1003 45 36 535 28 28 ``` ::: ::: The command `nobs(val_model)` gives the number of observations $n$ that the model uses, here 874. Twenty-five deals have standardised residuals beyond $\pm 3$, and 64 have a Cook's distance above $4/n$. These are 3% and 7% of the 874 deals. The most influential deal claimed a valuation of \$50 million and was agreed at \$25 million, half of the claim. Its claimed valuation lies far from the claimed valuations of the other deals. Such an observation has high leverage: like a long lever, it can pull the fitted line towards itself. @fig-i02-influence marks the 64 deals in the scatterplot. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="See the R code for this figure"} library(ggplot2) sharks <- read.csv("data/shark_tank_teaching.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE) vals <- subset(sharks, deal_on_show == 1 & deal_equity_pct > 0) vals$claimed_m <- vals$requested_valuation_usd / 1e6 vals$agreed_m <- vals$deal_valuation_usd / 1e6 val_model <- lm(agreed_m ~ claimed_m, data = vals) cd <- cooks.distance(val_model) vals$flagged <- cd > 4 / nrow(vals) top <- which.max(cd) ggplot(vals, aes(x = claimed_m, y = agreed_m)) + geom_point(data = subset(vals, !flagged), colour = "grey75", alpha = 0.45, size = 1.6) + geom_abline(intercept = coef(val_model)[1], slope = coef(val_model)[2], colour = "#D55E00", linewidth = 0.9) + geom_point(data = subset(vals, flagged), colour = "#D55E00", size = 2.2) + annotate("text", x = vals$claimed_m[top] - 1.2, y = vals$agreed_m[top], label = "claimed 50, agreed 25", hjust = 1, colour = "#17324D", size = 3.4) + labs(x = "Valuation claimed by the founder ($ millions)", y = "Valuation agreed on air ($ millions)") + theme_minimal(base_size = 13) + theme( panel.grid.minor = element_blank(), panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(), plot.caption = element_text(colour = "#5B6976"), axis.title = element_text(colour = "#17324D") ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![The 874 deals with the fitted line, full range shown. Orange points have a Cook's distance above 4/n. The labelled deal (claimed $50 million, agreed $25 million) moves the fitted line most: it sits far to the right (high leverage), so it pulls on the line like a lever.](i02-assumptions-diagnostics_files/figure-html/fig-i02-influence-1.png){#fig-i02-influence width=672} ::: ::: What should you do with a flagged observation? Follow three steps, in this order: 1. **Investigate.** Is it a data error, or a real pitch? Here the valuations of the flagged deals match their recorded amounts and shares, so we treat these deals as real. 2. **Report.** State that the results depend on a few observations and say which ones. Show the fit with and without them if the results change. 3. **Never silently delete.** If you drop rows that do not fit your story and do not say so, you give a false picture of the data. ### Q--Q plots: how to read them, when normality matters [Shark Tank data]{.shark-tag} The fifth row of the table is normality of the errors. A **normal Q--Q plot** (quantile-quantile plot) puts the standardised residuals in order and compares them with the values that a normal distribution would give. If the residuals are close to normal, the points lie along the reference line. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="See the R code for this figure"} library(ggplot2) sharks <- read.csv("data/shark_tank_teaching.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE) vals <- subset(sharks, deal_on_show == 1 & deal_equity_pct > 0) vals$claimed_m <- vals$requested_valuation_usd / 1e6 vals$agreed_m <- vals$deal_valuation_usd / 1e6 val_model <- lm(agreed_m ~ claimed_m, data = vals) qq_df <- data.frame(rs = rstandard(val_model)) ggplot(qq_df, aes(sample = rs)) + geom_qq_line(colour = "#D55E00", linewidth = 0.9) + geom_qq(colour = "#009E73", alpha = 0.4, size = 1.6) + labs(x = "Normal theoretical quantile", y = "Standardised residual") + theme_minimal(base_size = 13) + theme( panel.grid.minor = element_blank(), panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(), plot.caption = element_text(colour = "#5B6976"), axis.title = element_text(colour = "#17324D") ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Normal Q--Q plot of the standardised residuals of the valuation model. Both ends leave the line: a few deals were agreed far above and far below their fitted valuation.](i02-assumptions-diagnostics_files/figure-html/fig-i02-qq-1.png){#fig-i02-qq width=672} ::: ::: The horizontal axis shows where a residual of this rank would lie if the errors were normal. The vertical axis shows where the residual actually lies. In @fig-i02-qq the middle of the distribution is close to the line. Both ends bend away from it, the upper end more strongly. The residuals have more extreme values on both sides than a normal distribution has. We say that such a distribution has heavy tails. Two base R commands draw the same plot without the styling of the figure: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} qqnorm(rstandard(val_model)) qqline(rstandard(val_model)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](i02-assumptions-diagnostics_files/figure-html/i02-qq-base-1.png){width=672} ::: ::: When does this matter? Normal errors are needed for exact t and F distributions in small samples. With 874 observations the tests and intervals of Lecture 3 still hold approximately without normal errors, because of the central limit theorem: averages over many observations are close to normal, and the estimated slope is such an average. The approximation is weaker when a few extreme deals decide where the line lies. Very extreme outliers distort both the line and its standard errors, in samples of any size. ::: {.caveat-box} What a residual check can and cannot show - A residual plot without patterns agrees with the assumptions. It does not prove them. An omitted confounder and dependent errors do not show up in a plot. - Heteroskedasticity or an influential deal is a finding to look into and to report. It is not a final judgement on the model. - Keeping or dropping an unusual observation is a decision that you make from knowledge of the data and that you state openly. **What you can do with it:** before you trust a fitted line, look at its residual plot and at the few points that move it most. If the conclusion changes without them, say so. ::: ### Answering the driving question You can trust the Lecture 1 line only under certain conditions. Its residuals reveal two problems. The vertical spread grows with the size of the claim (heteroskedasticity). And a few extreme deals, flagged by standardised residuals beyond $\pm3$ and Cook's distances above $4/n$, strongly affect both the line and its standard errors. Heteroskedasticity does not bias the slope, but it makes the usual standard errors doubtful. Nothing in the plots contradicts linearity. Independence and zero conditional mean (no omitted confounder) cannot be seen in any plot. They depend on how the show works. Without zero conditional mean, the slope describes how agreed valuations differ across claims, but it is not the effect of claiming more. Lecture 3 calculates standard errors, intervals, and tests for this model. These two problems limit how much you can trust those results. ::: {.founder-box} A founder's decision (invented example) One week in your data includes a catering order of 200 meal boxes, in a week with high advertising. With that week the advertising slope is 0.15. Without that week the slope is 0.09. The decision: do not base next term's budget on a fit that depends on one single week. Catering is a different business from selling single meal boxes every day. You report both fits, plan the daily business with the slope of 0.09, and look at catering separately. ::: **Next:** The slope is an estimate from one set of deals. Lecture 3 shows how precise it is, with its standard error, its confidence interval, and a t-test. It also shows how much of the variation in the outcome the line explains ($R^2$) and how to test whether the model is useful at all (the F-test). ::: ::: {.course-phase .phase-after} ## After class After the lecture, work through all the practice below. ### Read the lecture material Read the Lecture material section above from start to end. The lecture covered the main points. The text has every step, every example, and all the code, including parts that were not shown in class. Note what is still unclear and bring it to the next tutorial, or ask Tilly. ### Recall questions 1. Which assumption says that the average of $Y$ at each value of $X$ lies on a straight line? 2. Must the outcome variable be normally distributed? Why or why not? 3. What does a fan shape in a residual-versus-fitted plot suggest? 4. Which assumptions can you not check with a residual plot alone? 5. What do a standardised residual and Cook's distance each measure? 6. What are the three steps for handling a flagged observation? 7. Which assumptions make the slope unbiased, and which assumptions do the usual standard errors need? ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Check your answers 1. Linearity, $E[Y\mid X=x]=\beta_0+\beta_1x$. 2. No. The assumptions are about the errors at each value of the predictor and about how the data were produced. They are not about the distribution of $Y$ or of $X$ on its own. 3. Heteroskedasticity: the variance of the errors is not constant. 4. Independence and zero conditional mean (no omitted confounder). They require knowledge of how the data were collected. A residual plot cannot show them, because least squares makes the residuals unrelated to $X$ even when the error terms are related to it. 5. A standardised residual measures how unusual one observation's residual is, in standard-deviation units. Cook's distance measures how much the whole fitted line moves if that observation is removed. 6. Investigate, report, never silently delete. 7. Unbiased slope: variation in $X$, linearity, independent observations, and zero conditional mean. Usual standard errors: homoskedasticity and independence. Normality of the errors is needed only for exact tests in small samples. ::: ### Finish a half-worked example: diagnose three residual plots For each panel of @fig-i02-three-plots, write one sentence: which assumption, if any, does the plot challenge? Plot A (given). The residuals follow a U shape. The average residual is negative in the middle and positive at the ends, so the plot challenges linearity. Plot B and Plot C (you). Write the sentence for each of them in the same way. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code code-fold="true" code-summary="See the R code for this figure"} library(ggplot2) set.seed(1204) n_p <- 120 f_p <- seq(1, 9, length.out = n_p) res_a <- 1.6 * (f_p - 5)^2 / 8 - 1 + rnorm(n_p, 0, 0.55) res_b <- rnorm(n_p, 0, 0.15 + 0.16 * f_p) res_c <- rnorm(n_p, 0, 0.8) plots_df <- data.frame( panel = rep(c("Plot A", "Plot B", "Plot C"), each = n_p), fitted = rep(f_p, 3), residual = c(res_a, res_b, res_c) ) zero_lab <- data.frame( panel = c("Plot A", "Plot B", "Plot C"), x = 1, y = c(max(res_a), max(res_b), max(res_c)) ) ggplot(plots_df, aes(x = fitted, y = residual)) + geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "#C98B2E", linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 0.8) + geom_point(alpha = 0.45, size = 1.6, colour = "#009E73") + geom_text(data = zero_lab, aes(x = x, y = y, label = "residual = 0"), hjust = 0, colour = "#17324D", size = 3) + facet_wrap(~ panel, scales = "free_y") + labs(x = "Fitted value", y = "Residual") + theme_minimal(base_size = 13) + theme( panel.grid.minor = element_blank(), panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(), plot.caption = element_text(colour = "#5B6976"), axis.title = element_text(colour = "#17324D"), strip.text = element_text(colour = "#17324D", face = "bold") ) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Three simulated residual-versus-fitted plots. The gold dashed line marks residual zero in each panel.](i02-assumptions-diagnostics_files/figure-html/fig-i02-three-plots-1.png){#fig-i02-three-plots width=672} ::: ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Check your answers Plot B: the vertical band widens with the fitted value. This fan shape shows heteroskedasticity, so it challenges homoskedasticity. Plot C: no visible pattern. The plot agrees with linearity and homoskedasticity, the two assumptions it can show. This result is not proof that all assumptions hold. ::: ### Practice: diagnostics for your own model [Shark Tank data]{.shark-tag} Regress the equity offered by the founder, in percent (`equity_offered_pct`), on the season (`season`), using all 1,441 pitches. Produce the residual-versus-fitted plot and the normal Q--Q plot. Interpret each in one or two sentences. Then count the standardised residuals beyond $\pm 3$ and the observations with a Cook's distance above $4/n$. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Check your answers ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} sharks <- read.csv("data/shark_tank_teaching.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE) equity_model <- lm(equity_offered_pct ~ season, data = sharks) old_par <- par(no.readonly = TRUE) par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4.5, 4.4, 1.3, 0.7), las = 1) plot(fitted(equity_model), residuals(equity_model), pch = 16, col = grDevices::adjustcolor("#0072B2", alpha.f = 0.30), bty = "n", xlab = "Fitted equity offered (pp)", ylab = "Residual (pp)") abline(h = 0, lty = 2, lwd = 2, col = "#D55E00") qqnorm(rstandard(equity_model), pch = 16, col = grDevices::adjustcolor("#009E73", alpha.f = 0.35), bty = "n", main = "", xlab = "Normal theoretical quantile", ylab = "Standardised residual") qqline(rstandard(equity_model), col = "#D55E00", lwd = 2) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](i02-assumptions-diagnostics_files/figure-html/i02-practice-equity-1.png){width=672} ::: ```{.r .cell-code} par(old_par) max(residuals(equity_model)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 82.83991 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} c(big_rstandard = sum(abs(rstandard(equity_model)) > 3), cooks_flagged = sum(cooks.distance(equity_model) > 4 / nobs(equity_model))) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` big_rstandard cooks_flagged 18 58 ``` ::: ::: The residual plot shows sixteen vertical stripes. The season (`season`) takes only whole-number values, so only sixteen fitted values exist. That is a feature of the predictor, not a violation. The vertical spread is broadly similar across the stripes, so there is no strong heteroskedasticity. The Q--Q plot bends upwards at the right end: some pitches offered far more equity than the fitted trend. The largest residual is about 83 percentage points, from founders who offered almost the whole company. So the normality assumption probably does not hold. With $n = 1441$ this matters little for tests and intervals, but you should look more closely at the extreme rows. Eighteen standardised residuals lie beyond $\pm 3$, and 58 pitches have a Cook's distance above $4/n$. These are about 1% and 4% of the 1,441 pitches. ::: ### Review questions from past lectures [Shark Tank data]{.shark-tag} Using the Lecture 1 fitted equation $\widehat{\text{agreed}} = -0.068 + 0.649 \times \text{claimed}$ (both in \$ millions): a founder claimed a valuation of \$3 million and the deal was agreed on air at \$1.5 million.
